NATIONAL PARKS, MAN.  EMPLOYMENT PROCEDURES
speechtext:
1.	Are employment procedures for the national parks in Manitoba different to those in effect in other provinces?
2.	If so, what are the differences, how long are they to be in effect, and what provisions are there to prevent discriminations?

speakeroldname: Hon. Alvin Hamilton (Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: NATIONAL PARKS, MAN.  EMPLOYMENT PROCEDURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is aware that the former member for the Marquette constituency was also the Manitoba minister in the Liberal 66968-9-43
government. Under that government, prevailing rates employees for Riding Mountain park were hired through local advisers rather than through the national employment service, the normal practice followed in other parks. During the first year in office the present government followed a similar procedure. However, this fall, in view of the vigorous winter work campaign, my office contacted the members for Marquette, Brandon-Souris and Dauphin, suggesting that every effort should be made to ensure that the most needy cases should be given first consideration in the national park area, irrespective of party affiliations. In this regard we were especially cognizant of the fact that many farmers live on submarginal land and had a complete crop failure in 1958. This also included farm labourers, who during the winter season are unemployed and do not come under the Unemployment Insurance Act.
Last fall the hon. member for Brandon-Souris was in touch with me following a meeting of the winter work committee for western Manitoba, suggesting that the hiring for national park projects should be done through the national employment offices adjacent to the park. Arrangements were made at that time to have the names of all the men seeking winter employment at the park registered in the Brandon national employment service office. Since the members have returned to Ottawa for the present session a meeting has been held with the Minister of Labour and the officials of the national employment service to regularize these procedures.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I ask leave to move the adjournment of the house under standing order No. 26 for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance, namely the most serious situation caused by unemployment and the lack of any major and immediate action being taken to alleviate the problem.
On the matter of urgency, Mr. Speaker, I may say that there are tens of thousands of unemployed who are not eligible to receive unemployment insurance payments, and of those there are many thousands who are not even entitled to receive social welfare payments. In the speech from the throne, and in the addresses given in the debate by members of the government since January 15, we have not noticed any intention on the part of the government to present to this parliament any substantial measures to handle the situation.
In the light of the present needs of our fellow citizens, in the light of the fact that nothing except minor legislation is expected, and in the light of the promise that no one in Canada will suffer because of unemployment, it is my hope that this house will agree to the need for a debate at this time.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: If any hon. member wishes to address himself to the question of the urgency of debate the matter proposed, I shall be glad to hear him.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader

May I point out, Mr. Speaker, that there was an amendment before this house for a period of nine days dealing with this very question, and the members of the C.C.F. as well as the members of the official opposition had ample opportunity to debate the question without limitation. They had practically no suggestions to make. This amendment was dealt with on Thursday last, and I suggest it was never the intention of the rules of the house that an hon. member could come in and have a second try at a question of this kind by moving the adjournment of the house within a matter of six days after such a vote.
Furthermore, I point out to your honour that the business before the house today is something having to do with this whole question of unemployment. I do submit that the motion is completely out of order.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
It is true that the subject of employment was discussed during the debate on the address, Mr. Speaker, but the very character of that particular


procedure is one that lends itself to the discussion of a wide variety of subjects. The hon. gentleman who now complains about the motion moved by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam was among those who resisted any suggestions that a full discussion on unemployment at that time was in the interests of the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
My hon. friend says oh, oh, but he and the Prime Minister were among those who said a discussion of the subject was not calculated to relieve the problem. What the hon. member has sought to do today is to focus our attention on unemployment, and not only on unemployment but on the fact that thousands of individuals are not capable of qualifying for unemployment insurance benefits or for seasonal benefits.
Since the government has not brought forward its legislation in this particular it would seem to me, Mr. Speaker, with great respect, in the light of the acknowledged fact that this is one of the foremost problems now confronting our country, that parliament ought to be given the opportunity, through the specific form of this motion, to deal with this urgent national question.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if I may I should like to say a word on this matter. We feel that this is a matter of urgency, and that it is urgent today. The fact that a motion was dealt with at some previous time has nothing to do with the cold, hard fact that hundreds of thousands of people in this country are unemployed, and it has nothing to do with the declaration we have put forward to the effect that the government should announce its policies to deal with this extremely urgent matter.
Another reason we advance in contending that it is urgent is the fact that we are receiving statements from the province of British Columbia-from the British Columbia federation of labour and other interested organizations and people in that province- pointing out that there is a real unemployment crisis. As to the urgency of this subject, Mr. Speaker, I might remind hon. members that there was a march on the legislative buildings in Victoria just the other day in order to impress upon the authorities the urgency of this extremely important problem.
We submit, Mr. Speaker, that the government should welcome a debate in parliament at this time on this urgent matter, and that they should welcome the opportunity to present their policy at this time.

ordinary course of proceedings for the purpose of a debate, not for coming to a decision, because the motion is to adjourn the house and it obviously settles or decides nothing. All it does is give hon. members the opportunity to debate a matter of urgent public importance.
Therefore I think the important consideration in dealing with motions of this kind is the urgency of debate. I do not propose to deal with the urgency of the unemployment problem. speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the National Housing Act, 1954, to increase from $750 million to $1 billion the aggregate amount that may be paid out of the consolidated revenue fund under subsection 1 of section 22 of the act, and to remove the limitation on the amount thereof that may be advanced to the corporation for the purposes of subsection 1 of section 11 of the said act, and to provide further for certain changes in connection with the administration of the act.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Sevigny in the chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENT INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT AVAILABLE, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this is a resolution preceding a bill to amend the National Housing Act. Hon. members will notice that the resolution covers a proposed increase from $750 million to $1 billion in the aggregate amount that may be paid out of the consolidated revenue fund under subsection 1 of section 22 of the act. It also provides for the removal of the limitation on the amount that can be advanced to the corporation for the purposes of subsection 1 of section 11 of the act, and in addition provides for certain other changes in connection with the administration of the act. I propose today to deal first with the increase in the money available under subsection 1 of section 22 of the act.
It will be remembered that when we took office in the summer of 1957 subsection 1 of section 22 made provision for an amount of $250 million. At the time about $100 million had already been used, and in view of the rapidly diminishing number of houses then being started and of the great need for homes for Canadians of moderate income, and also to help the house-building industry and to provide employment, we decided to use the remaining $150 million then available primarily for the support of a new policy which we described as a small home loan policy.
I do not need to go into all the details of that plan today. We set a limit on the size of 66968-9-44J
National Housing Act
house on which a loan could be made, that limit being 1,050 square feet for a house with three bedrooms. Furthermore, the method of making these loans was to have them handled through the various lending institutions. In other words it was in reality an agency plan.
As a result there was a great increase in the construction of small homes in Canada, and in December, 1957, we asked for an additional $150 million, bringing the total available under subsection 1 of section 22 to $400 million. In May of 1958 the house voted an additional $350 million, and that is how we arrived at the total sum of $750 million now available under the act. Mind you, this money was not all drawn for small home loans, because under this section we also finance limited dividend rental housing projects, and the section also provides for housing assistance in connection with primary industries.
As of January 30, 1959, a total of $677,956,248 had been committed. That means that as of approximately a week ago there remained in the fund $72,043,752.
It is interesting to note that under the agency plan there was a total of approximately $280 million used. This, of course, is all for the small homes. We dropped the agency plan, by the way, last May and then adopted the policy of lending direct from Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation for these small homes. In addition, throughout the whole period, this crown corporation has been lending direct in the smaller centres in Canada, and many of these loans came out of the amounts I have mentioned. The total for direct loans by the corporation is $213,817,292. Perhaps I should give the exact figure for the agency loans, and it is $279,117,169.
The total figure for the limited dividend fund is $117,912,742, and of that $52,169,054 has been committed since January, 1958. Hon. members will notice that there is a further amount under that limited dividend plan, some of which was committed before we took office. Actually, the amount since January, 1958, is $52,169,054. Then for primary industry housing the total is $6,343,519. We have not been making use of this primary industry plan at all. There may have been one or two advances when we first took over, but since then we have not been using money for this purpose.
Hon. members might be interested in noting that during the calendar year 1958 Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation committed $388 million for housing, and in the same period of time the private lending institutions, including the banks, committed $520 million. The result of the policy has

National Housing Act
been that in 1958 there has been a tremendous increase in the number of housing starts. About a year ago I forecast with some trepidation that there might be 140,000. This, of course, would have been a record because the highest year before that was 1955 when there were 138,276. However, things have gone very well and I now have the final figures for 1958. They are even better than the announcement made last week or the week before in the house. The total number of starts was 164,632, and this is about 42,000 more than in the calendar year 1957. As hon. members will see, it is more than 26,000 above the record of 1955.
Completions for 1958 numbered 146,686. This again is a record and above the highest figure before, which was in 1956, namely 135,700. At the end of the year, there were under construction 88,162 houses. This, again, is a record, the previous high being 79,339. As I pointed out, one of the main objectives was to help create employment by this housing policy. There can be no doubt but that house-building in 1958 has set the pace for all activities in Canada. It has been in the forefront of the economic activity in Canada. We estimate that during the year there were probably 200,000 man-years of employment provided by on-site construction alone. This means about 400,000 jobs because it takes about six months to build a home.
Then, in addition, there have been all the jobs more remotely involved in the construction of housing units of various kinds. For example, there is the ground servicing of the land, the production, handling and transportation of building materials, bringing the total to about 400,000 man-year jobs. There are, as well, the men employed in getting out the logs, lumbering, the making of furniture and the equipment which goes into a home. By the way, I noticed that the vice-president of Simpson-Sears Limited, Mr. Morgan Reid, is quoted as saying a few days ago that these new homes represent a potential demand for furnishings and equipment estimated at $1,700 to $2,000 per house. Hon. members can calculate for themselves just what house-building has meant to Canada during the last year. I do not think anyone will quarrel with my submission that the government's housing policy has been largely responsible for this result which has been so beneficial to our nation.
In the United States there was also an increase in housing activity during last year. But in the United States they were much below their previous record which was made in 1955 just as the previous record in Canada had been in 1955. In 1955 they had 1,328,900 houses started and in 1958 it was estimated they had 1,170,000.
There has been some suggestion that too many houses were being built and that they would become a glut on the market. I have read that comment in some of the papers. This is a factor which we have had very much in mind during the whole of 1958. There would not have been much point in rushing the construction of small homes if there were going to be too many of them, thereby causing the whole market to be broken.
The figures for completed and unoccupied dwellings are as follows: December, 1958, 3,212. I may say this is for the whole of Canada and I would ask hon. members to keep in mind that this is after this record number of houses had been completed. In 1957 that figure was 2,764 or only about 450 more at the end of 1958 than at the end of 1957. In some centres there are actually less. For example, in the Toronto metropolitan area there was more housing going on in that year than in any other part of Canada. In December, 1958 there were 970 of these completed and unoccupied houses in the Toronto metropolitan area whereas in 1957 there were 1,146.
Then we have tried hard to increase the home building in the smaller centres of Canada. I would point out that the great demand is in the metropolitan areas. However, we have gone out deliberately to increase construction in the smaller centres. The Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation officials wrote to every municipality with a population of 1,500 and over pointing out what could be done, the facilities available in obtaining loans and offering to send an official to that municipality for the purpose of discussing the position with those holding office. We have had considerable success with that program as a result.
Of the housing starts in 1958 there were 56,673 in centres with populations under 30,000 compared with 49,673 in 1957, an increase of 13.78 per cent. Of the number of units approved under the National Housing Act in 1958, 19,471 were approved in centres with under 30,000 population compared with 13,488 in 1958, an increase of 44.4 per cent. In addition, the corporation got out special plans for very modest homes. A great many of those have been called for and a large number of these very cheap homes are now being constructed across the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENT INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT AVAILABLE, ETC.
speechtext:
That is 848 square feet.
Then in Moncton, New Brunswick, one builder has for some years been building houses in a price range of under $10,000. In 1958 he completed 100 houses with prices ranging from $8,500 to $9,900, down payments from $650 to $900. While these houses bear no relationship to the C.M.H.C. plan they are minimum in size and they have complete plumbing, heating and electrical wiring and full basements.

Three of the $7,900 houses are built to a plan similar to the national home builders association budget research house.
I should like to say a few words about the people who have benefited by the small home loan plan. We find that the largest percentage is in the group with income from

the answers but this is a vital activity of government and we would appreciate any helpful suggestions.
I should now say a word or two about the other amendments which are proposed. They will be designed to make National Housing Act mortgages as attractive as possible to private investors. Some lenders whose powers of investment extend to securities guaranteed by the government of Canada have felt that N.H.A. insured loans did not fall into this category because the insurance fund guaranteed only 98 per cent and not 100 per cent of the face value of the mortgage. We believe that by eliminating the 2 per cent reduction-it is commonly called the "2 per cent bite", I believe, in the business-the National Housing Act will permit trustees of pension funds, executors, trust companies and other private sources of investment to contribute to capital investment in housing.
Because of its extensive direct lending operations during the last 18 months Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is developing a substantial mortgage portfolio. Under one of the amendments these mortgages would be available for sale to investors who are willing to invest in the housing field but who are unable to make loans themselves. The amendment proposes to permit C.M.H.C. to sell these loans to such private investors. I believe the corporation can now sell these loans to an approved lender such as a bank or mortgage company but it cannot sell the mortgages to any company which is not an approved lender. Under the amendment it will be possible to do that because Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation will be given the power to administer these particular loans.
Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation may wish at times to buy more mortgages. Under the present law it can use only the $25 million for that purpose. We are taking out the restriction on the amount of money the corporation can spend in buying mortgages from approved lenders. There is also to be a change which will increase from $125 to $150 the amount allowed in calculating the payment to an approved lender who has made a claim on the insurance fund. The basic purpose of the insurance feature of the act is to protect the mortgagee against loss in such a case. Experience has shown that the legal cost generally exceeds the $120 previously allowed. This change would not, of course, affect the position of the liability of the borrower who has defaulted on his mortgage account.

First of all, I should like to compliment the minister on the complete and comprehensive statement he has just given the committee and for that we are grateful. I may say that I think most hon. members regardless of where they sit in the house, would share with him in what he has said about the importance of house-building generally. I am very pleased to be able to say that the minister has shown a rather complete knowledge of his subject and we do appreciate the time that he has given us today. I am pleased to have the opportunity of paying this compliment to the minister because, as he may know, or at least I want him to know, he is one of my favourite ministers.
Another point I should like to make is that we appreciate the attitude the minister displayed in his statement to the committee and the absence to a great degree of political references and for that I wish to compliment him.
I should like to say that the Liberals have always-I think this applies, of course, to most parties-favoured more and better housing for our people. I do not think any of us has to take a back seat in that regard. So far as the Liberal party is concerned, we had a particularly proud record during the years we were in office.
I would like to congratulate the government upon its activities in the housing field in direct proportion to the degree to which those actions may have stimulated house construction and the economy in a period of economic slowdown.
There are a few questions that I had hoped we would have the answers to today. One of them, of course, the minister was kind enough to answer, namely how much money was available. I think he said it was something of the order of $72 million. That leads us to the next question. Will the funds that we are discussing today aid employment this winter? At the rate the money is being invested at the present time it seems hardly likely that the funds we are discussing today will have any appreciable effect on unemployment this winter.
