subtopic: AMENDMENT INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT AVAILABLE, ETC.
speechtext:
I appreciate the remarks the minister has made. The point I was trying to make was that there is a substantial amount of money available at the present time, so that the money we are discussing today, added to that fund, does not in that sense aid projects that might at this moment of time be held up. That is the only point I wanted to make.
There is a third matter with which some of us are concerned, namely precisely how much of the money we are discussing today will be put into low-priced houses and into low-rental houses? Precisely what will be the percentage?
The fourth point is, what plans, if any, does the government have to help counteract the greatest problem in the house-building industry, namely the ever-soaring cost of land? I would have liked to hear the minister say something on that point?
The fifth point I would like to make at this time is that we would have appreciated a forecast from the minister because, in spite of what he might say and the arguments he might advance, the substantial sums of money that we are discussing now that the government through its agency, Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, is putting into the construction industry mean that they are continuing to take over a larger part of the financing of house-building. A statement in that regard, as to the objective of the government, the number of starts that might be made in 1959, would be helpful.

Before going further, Mr. Chairman, I
should like to take the opportunity that this discussion affords me to offer my congratulations and those of the hon. members on this side of the house to those members of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation who have over these many years done such an excellent job.
At this time I should like to point out that the official opposition supports in the main the government's activities that have a beneficial effect on the number of housing units produced. However, having regard to the large number of starts in 1958, one cannot help wondering how much is due to the fact that the construction industry, in many fields, was depressed; second, that the many millions poured into housing by the government were obviously to bolster our sagging economy. However, I do not wish to minimize the results in any way and I will not pursue this point further at this time.
When we read the resolution before us it is evident that the government has three broad purposes in mind: first, to increase from $750 million to $1 billion the amount that may be paid out of the consolidated revenue fund under subsection 1 of section 22 of the act; second, to remove the limitation on the amount that may be advanced to the corporation for the purposes of subsection 1 of section 11 of the said act; and, third, to provide for certain changes in connection with the administration of the act.
May I say at once that we in the official opposition will at this stage support the resolution which in effect gives the government leave to introduce the bill. We will support the government in all its activities in this important field that will, in our opinion, have the effect of making better housing available to our people. At the same time we will take advantage of the opportunities afforded in this debate to point out some of the danger signs that we see with respect to the situation generally and the government's activities in particular.
Speaking directly to the resolution, I should like to say a few words about part 1, the proposed increase from $750 million to $1 billion. Section 22 was first enacted as part of the National Housing Act in 1954. As originally enacted, section 22 established a limit of $250 million on the amount that might be paid to the corporation out of the consolidated revenue fund. This amount was increased from $250 million to $400 million in December, 1957.
At this point it might be of some interest if I were to refer to two conflicting statements made by the Minister of Finance on
National Housing Act
this subject. The first statement was made at Murray Bay in June, 1958, when he stated:
During 1957, however, the competition for loan funds became less competitive as the year progressed and more important, in August and again in September government funds in a total amount of $300 million were made available to augment loan funds supplied by insurance companies, banks and private lenders.
The second statement of the Minister of Finance to which I should like to refer was made at the Canadian Club early this year, on January 5, I believe. At that time he said, dealing with the same period of time:
In the second half of 1957 the competition for loan funds from other investment outlets became less intense, and over half a billion dollars of government funds were made available to augment housing loans supplied by the private lenders.
An examination of the facts would indicate that in August, 1957-I think the minister confirmed this again today-about $100 million of the $250 million provided for under section 22 of the National Housing Act had been used and the amount was increased by way of an amendment passed in December, 1957. The amount provided for under section 22 was increased from $250 million to $400 million, so that the first statement by the Minister of Finance that $300 million were made available is correct but not the statement made at the Canadian Club. A further increase from $400 million to $750 million was made early in 1958 and the proposed increase now brings the limit to $1 billion.
Section 22 gives the minister the authority, with the approval of the governor in council, out of the consolidated revenue fund, to (a) advance moneys to the corporation for the purpose of making loans under part 2 of the act, which deals with housing for rental purposes and land assembly, and under section 40, which enables the corporation to lend where loans are not available; (b) to reimburse the corporation for loss sustained in respect of loans made under part 2 of the act, that is, houses for rental purposes and land assembly; (c) to advance moneys, to the corporation, not in excess of $25 million, for the purposes of subsection 1 of section 11, which enables the corporation, either out of its reserve fund or out of moneys appropriated by section 22, to purchase all right or interest of a holder of an insured loan, and to make loans to a private lender on the security of an assignment or an agreement to assign an insured loan. Up to the present time the amendments which have been adopted have related only to the increase in the amount that may be made available to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and not to the purpose for which this amount may be used.

National Housing Act
Without in any way minimizing any action that the government may have taken with respect to housing I think it is only fair to point out that in the past year the government has borrowed very substantial sums and that it is obvious that some of this money was provided by investors who might otherwise have used the funds in question for mortgage investment. In a review of Canadian housing statistics, third quarter, 1958, it is stated that the lending institutions in the first nine months of 1958 approved mortgage loans of all kinds amounting to nearly $900 million, more than in any corresponding period of any previous year. I think it is only reasonable to suggest that they might have lent substantially more if they had not been asked to subscribe to the government's bonds, which increased the national debt. Quite obviously, to the extent that the government has borrowed money from institutions which might themselves have used it for mortgage loans, Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and through it the government have taken over the function which might have been fulfilled to a larger degree by private and institutional lenders themselves.
Up to the end of the third quarter of 1958 Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation had approved mortgages amounting to nearly $700 million so that it was left with this relatively small fund to which the minister referred as being approximately $72 million. Consequently, we believe that we cannot object to increasing the amount at its disposal from $750 million to $1 billion as the corporation should be in a position to speed up or slow down its lending activities, having regard at all times to economic conditions and the desirability of encouraging further new residential construction.
There are two aspects of the problem to which I think it is appropriate that some consideration be given and upon which some comment might be made during this discussion. First, whatever amounts are lent by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation in excess of repayments received on loans already made by it represent additional new money which must be raised by the government. In other words, the government's cash requirements will be increased by the amount of any new money which is advanced to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
As a member of the opposition I am in no position, at least at this stage of the session, to know what the over-all cash requirements of the government will be for 1959-60. However, I think it is correct to say that the experience of the government since the beginning of the current fiscal year in raising new money is such that it ought to be particularly

conscious of the dangers inherent in increasing its cash requirements at this time. As we know, since last May the government has borrowed very substantial sums but only a small part of its requirements has been represented by long term loans subscribed to and paid for out of savings.
The government may attempt to point to the success of the last savings bond campaign but this is hardly the type of money that should be borrowed for mortgage financing. Canada savings bonds are demand obligations and not long term bonds. I believe I am correct in saying that of all the large quantity of bonds sold in 1958 only $350 million represent long term bonds. There is a very direct link between the amounts advanced to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation for mortgage investment and the cash requirements of the government.
The second aspect in connection with any governmental mortgage program is that the government itself may not be as sensitive to the need or demand for new housing as individual lenders may be. The individual lenders are risking their own money and they have to be right. They cannot afford to be making loans on houses that are not going to sell. I make this comment only to point out that the government's view with regard to mortgage lending may be influenced by purely economic factors, that is, the desirability to keep the industry in high gear in order to provide employment. It should be pointed out that inasmuch as the government itself is a lender, losses resulting from overexpansion of the supply of a certain class of houses will fall not upon the shoulders of the government itself but upon the shoulders of those who build them or buy them.
In other words, there are two important factors to be considered. The first is the desirability of providing employment, and the second is the advisability or inadvisability of constructing a further supply of houses within any given period. The choice of appropriate policies, and the turning on or turning off of lending operations are responsibilities that must rest with the government itself.
During the past six years very substantial progress has been made, and I think it is only fair to say thanks to aggressive Liberal policies, including the adoption of the National Housing Act, 1954, and the introduction of the chartered banks into the mortgage lending field. In that period during which the Liberals were in office very substantial progress was made. I know the Conservative government will be quick to interject that more spectacular progress was made in

1958. However, I would remind the Conservative government that what was accomplished under the Liberal administration was done at a time of intense activity in the field of non-residential construction, when expansion of our natural and manufacturing resources was in most cases overtaxing our productive capacity.
I think it is only fair to say that what was done by the Conservatives in 1958 was done at a time when industrial activity had slackened off. During the six-year period from 1953 to 1958 inclusive net family formations amounted to 513,200, while 724,700 dwelling units were built. The estimated figures for 1958 show approximately 70,000 more homes were built than new families formed. This is a condition which clearly requires careful attention. I think that it must be obvious that conditions in one urban area will not necessarily correspond with those in other areas. I would suggest, for that reason, that mortgage lending activities of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation must be carefully watched. I would point out that this is a government responsibility and, as I see it, the responsibility of the opposition should surely not go beyond indicating at this stage the dangers that may be encountered.
The second phase of the resolution calls for the removal of the limitation on the amount that may be advanced to the corporation for the purposes of subsection 1 of section 11 of the act. It is not my intention to deal with this aspect of the proposed legislation at the resolution stage. At the moment, I can see no objection to giving Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation more resources so that it can be more active in buying and selling insured loans, although I think that perhaps we might reasonably question the desirability of such operations being carried out at the present time. I do not think this is a time when the government should be borrowing from investors, or worse still from the Bank of Canada, in order to acquire the mortgage investments of private lenders. However, lest there be any misunderstanding, I hasten to say that we welcome any legislation that would have the effect of making mortgage investments more negotiable. I would say that this is part of Liberal policy. I would refer to page 31 of the "Statement of Liberal Policy, 1958", where we stated that we stood for measures to make it easier for people to own their own homes, and one of the points emphasized reads as follows, "by further increasing the supply of mortgage money".
All of us realize that one of the greatest difficulties in the house-building industry can
National Housing Act
be the lack of a steady flow of mortgage funds which permit longer term planning and a more or less continuous flow of construction. This continuity of construction can mean reductions in builders' overhead and, as a result, would have the effect of lowering the cost to the house-buying public. There are many aspects of housing that I should like to discuss, but there will be other opportunities as this proposed legislation progresses through the house.
I would, perhaps, remind the government of the charges being made in some quarters that the National Housing Act money is being squandered on high priced homes which are a glut on the market. The minister referred to those charges today. Charges are continually popping up in our newspapers that luxury homes are being built with money supplied by the taxpayers. Such charges were made quite recently when the government announced that another $250 million was to be provided.
I mention this only to bring me to my next point. I am sure the government is well aware of the fact that there is an ever increasing need for low priced homes. The Canadian housing statistics report, third quarter, 1958, states on page 16 that the average borrower's income was well over $5,000 in the case of small home loans and nearly $6,000 in the category of other loans. It must be recognized, as I mentioned in this house on an earlier occasion, that the facilities of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, in spite of the good work it has done, are not meeting the needs of approximately 50 per cent of our people for housing. I am referring now to the 50 per cent of our people on the lower side of the income scale. I had hoped that the government would say more today concerning plans for filling this great need for housing for those people whose income is less than $4,000 per year. After all, the average weekly earnings in Canada today are approximately $70 per week. What greater proof is required to establish the fact that our housing program, despite the large number of starts that have been made over the years, today is not adequately meeting our requirements in the low priced field.
Personally, I would have liked to have seen a substantial portion of this $250 million referred to in the resolution earmarked specifically for low priced homes. I think, too, many Canadians will be disappointed to learn that the government does not propose any lowering of the interest rate on low rental housing projects. Here again is an opportunity to do something constructive toward meeting the need for housing among our lower income groups.

National Housing Act
I should like at this point to refer very briefly to a newspaper article that appeared in today's Montreal Gazette, having to do with a low cost housing project proposed for Cuba. I am not going to delay the house by reading the article, but the meat of the story is that a group of Montreal businessmen propose to invest something of the order of $80 million to $100 million in Cuba in low cost homes. Surely there must be something wrong when in view of the great need that exists today in this country for low cost housing that money is not being put to work in this country. Other members on this side will be dealing with other aspects of the proposed legislation. I will close by saying that we will support the resolution, and do everything possible within the limits of our responsibilities as an opposition, to facilitate its early passage through the house.

subtopic: AMENDMENT INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT AVAILABLE, ETC.
speechtext:
The item before the house at the moment, Mr. Chairman, is certainly one of considerable importance and weight. I think this has been demonstrated by the fact that both the Liberal and C.C.F. parties put up for their first speakers the weightiest men they have in their groups. I should like to add my voice to that of the hon. member for Nipissing in expressing my personal respect and the respect of this group of the minister for the job he has done in the past in the housing field. This is one branch of government activity that has certainly shown a marked improvement in the last year. This improvement has provided benefits in other fields as well, such as the field of employment, the supplementary industries and that sort of thing.
I believe the minister was being a bit modest when he gave credit for this improvement to the government. I feel that quite possibly the minister could take more credit, because had the credit been due to the government I am sure other branches would have shown a similar increase. Unfortunately, they have not done so. I believe, therefore, the minister could claim more credit than he appeared to wish to take at this time.
In spite of the progress and the good things we have heard about the minister and his department in this field, it is the job of the opposition to point out the weaknesses. That is what I intend to do this afternoon. The minister has outlined very well the benefits accruing from this particular project and I think that my duty should be to point out some of its faults and weaknesses. I think that the No. 1 fault with this program is that it does not look far enough ahead. I know that "planning" is a bad word to use in this House of Commons. However, I think it is a good one. When the government have talked so much to the Canadian people in the last

year about this long range planning for this northern vision, I think they should realize that in this field of housing there should be some long range planning as well or else we shall find that the housing situation, as it develops as the years go by, with the problems that we meet with now and will meet at an increased rate in the future, will certainly not fit into that vision that has been painted for the Canadian people.
I also believe that another fault which, if it is not equally important in connection with this program is certainly extremely important is the fact that it is a National Housing Act. However, unfortunately, at some place along the line we seem to have lost sight of the goal and we find that the secondary aspects of this program appear to be coming first in order instead of the way they should be. To back this up I should like to refer you, Mr. Chairman, to the words of the minister uttered just a few moments ago when he said that the prime purpose of this program was to help create employment. It is true that employment is extremely important and that it is badly needed at this time. However, the fact still remains that this is a housing act, not an employment act. I think possibly that has been one of the things wrong with this act which has prevented it from being as great a boon to the Canadian people as it could possibly be. In fact, it appears that to a great many people of this country employment and business interests come ahead of the actual goal of housing itself which certainly should be the goal under this act. This tendency is pointed out in the report of the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects, "Housing and Social Capital", at page two. I should like to read from this report in order to point out this particular point. I read from the bottom paragraph as follows:
Thus, when people want money spent on social capital, they will as often as not attempt to justify the outlay on the grounds of usefulness to industry. University spokesmen, for example, may suggest that a timely industrial donation now will yield good dividends of scientists, engineers and executives in the future.
Then on the next page it goes on to say this:
Indeed, one might argue that it is the industrial component of capital which is ancillary to the social, rather than the other way round. Industry and industrial organization are, after all, primarily a means to an end. But social capital and its associated institutions are both this and more. They relate, in part, to what is meant by civilization in the highest sense: they are worth having in themselves; they justify industry even as they facilitate it.
I think that is one thing that we are possibly losing sight of. I think it is certainly a thing to which we should give more thought. I

think the government should take this matter into consideration and should realize that, after all, this act is basically meant to provide housing for the Canadian people who need it and not necessarily merely to provide industry with a shot in the arm or to relieve unemployment when it reaches alarming proportions.
The realization of this need of planning, this need of long range thinking on this matter, is not something that is confined necessarily to this group. As far back as 1956 we find that the former minister of public works, namely Hon. Robert H. Winters, as reported at page 3301 of Hansard of April 26, 1956; had this to say:
The growth of cities has placed new demands upon the hearts of urban areas, with increasing traffic, growing commerce and a changed pattern of living. But during the last 10 years the prior need to build new suburbs did not permit any concerted action to conserve and replace the existing stock of the nation's housing.
Even then, the former minister realized that there was some definite need of some long range planning and study in connection with the problem of housing in our country. But unfortunately, to recognize something and to do something about it are not necessarily always one and the same thing. The past government and, unfortunately, this government on some occasions have come out and recognized problems but have not proceeded to do much about them. In order to give some further proof that planning is needed I should like to refer again to this report of the royal commission at page 31 where we find the following:
Thus, according to the forecast, the 1980 population of Canada would be 79 per cent urban, compared with 62 per cent in 1951. Montreal and Toronto might have populations of between 2.5 million and 3 million each, and Vancouver might have attained something between 1 million and 1.5 million.
This is where these problems are really going to crop up. We have seen them in the past; we are seeing them today and we are going to see them in the future with increasing frequency unless some far-reaching view is taken of this matter. All that a steady, progressive increase in the money for housing is going to do is to create crisis after crisis in our cities throughout this country as our population swings more and more from rural areas to urban areas. Unless some thought is given to planning for this change we are going to find ourselves in trouble in city after city across the country. This point is clearly brought out in this report of the royal commission to which I have made reference. I should like to quote from the remarks of Mr. Anthony Adamson, as found at page 40 of this report. He says this:
National Housing Act
Now we who live in the suburbs are, in the Canadian ethos, the cream of the crop. We are the worthwhile people. We are the solid Canadian way. In other words, we believe in home-ownership and the single-family detached house. To own a singlefamily detached house with $11,000 on a N.H.A. mortgage requires an income of $3,986 a year. The income of the average worker in a factory is $3,104 a year.
I might say, that he is here referring specifically to the Toronto area. The quotation continues:
So the average worker can't very well be a home-owner and the cream of the crop. He has to live in an old house or part of an old house on Ossington and drive out of Toronto to a factory in Etobicoke to go to work, while a decent homeowner in Etobicoke has to drive in to an office in Toronto to go to work. This sport is called "Rush Hour'' and it gives more people cardio-vascular-renal disease than fluoridation. It is also played on strips of concrete which cost a million dollars a mile to construct.
That points out, Mr. Chairman, some of the problems with which we are continually going to be faced unless some thought is given to this aspect of the policy. The principle is that housing is to help industry rather than industry helping housing. It means that we are using the goal to the road instead of the road to the goal.
Another aspect of this item which I think should receive some criticism is the fact that it creates inequalities for the people of this country. The hon. member for Nipissing dealt with that briefly. It was also shown in the last item I quoted from this report that by far the greatest majority of the working people of this country cannot qualify to make use of this National Housing Act in its past and present terms.
I will grant that the government did in the last session take one little step in the right direction when they introduced the minimum house, but again we had inequalities. For example, in the part of the country which I come from the standards of this minimum house do not meet with the local standards required by the municipalities. In an area of extreme weather temperatures you cannot get away with a house as outlined in this particular phase of the act. In fact we find, in some estimates which I have seen that close to 90 per cent of working people of this country cannot qualify under this particular act, and that only the top 10 per cent of the income bracket can take full advantage of it. As a result, as the hon. minister has pointed out today, reports have come to light that there is alarm in certain quarters that there is going to be a glut on the market with regard to this particular 10 per cent of the income bracket of the people of this country.
I have here a copy of the Montreal Gazette for Wednesday, January 28, and I would like

National Housing Act
to read one paragraph from an article by Mr. John Meyer, the financial editor. He states that:
Towards the end of the year, the number of houses purchased began to decline. A definite surplus was apparent at the year end.
Now as far as that particular item is concerned, I am sure the hon. minister is more familiar with it than I am myself. I merely want to point out that there is a feeling in certain quarters across this country that this particular group who have been able to take full advantage of this act in the past is approaching the position of having a glut on the market, which is all the more reason why the government should look for ways and means to make the housing act available to the lower income bracket people who need accommodation.
Then we also have another aspect of this act which I think leads to inequalities, that is, inequalities as far as participation by various provinces in this country is concerned. To illustrate that I have here a copy of the 12th annual report of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, and on page 39 of this report there is a table showing housing units under this act which have been completed by the provinces in 1957. These are, apparently the latest figures which they have to date. I will not read the whole table, but I would like to refer to two particular provinces, the province of Ontario and the province of Newfoundland. We find that in Ontario in that year the housing units started under the act amounted to 25,450; other than under the act, 22,289. This means that in the province of Ontario there were more housing units started under the act than with money provided from other sources. For that same year, in the province of Newfoundland there were only 239 housing units started under the act, while from other sources there was a total of 906. There is a variation in other provinces across the country, and I think there is a very good reason why this is so. I think it can be easily found by a comparison of the wage rates in various provinces across this country. It is borne out in the "Canadian Statistical Review for 1958", where we find that the average wage rate in Ontario is $73.40, while down in the maritimes, for example in the province of Nova Scotia, it is $58.65.
I think that points out very clearly that the act, as presently constituted, is not fair and equal to all Canadians across the country, and I think that before it can be so some further thought, study and action is required in regard to this act before it becomes equally applicable and of equal benefit to all Canadians.

Now there is another aspect, Mr. Chairman, which I think needs some attention. I suggest there has been far too much in the past, particularly in the field of low rental houses, of old-fashioned buck passing between provinces, municipalities and the federal government. One would help the other if the other helped him, and if the other helped him, and so on. It goes round in a merry circle and finally ends up in the lap of the municipalities, and unfortunately most of the municipalities are not in a position to do anything about it. I think the federal government should take a little more lead in this particular field in trying to look after this aspect of the housing problem.
There was another point mentioned by the hon. member for Nipissing and that was the complete lack of, I might even say, recognition of the high cost of land for housing. There was no hint on the part of the government, or in the minister's presentation, that the government was taking any notice whatsoever of land profiteering, the dreadfully high cost of real estate which in many areas is hamstringing, or badly crippling, our housing program and our housing needs. I believe that this is something which is of vital importance. I suggest that the federal government, who of course have to draw their money from the people of Canada, should be particularly careful that grasping and unscrupulous individuals across the country do not take advantage of any projects on which they embark. The federal government has a duty cast upon them to do everything in their power to ensure that the maximum benefit to the maximum number of people is gained from projects such as this.
Now, Mr. Chairman, other members in this group will be dealing with the other particular aspects of this item. There is one more point I should like to make before I conclude my remarks. This again ties in with what I said first about the need of taking a long range view with regard to housing needs and problems in Canada. It relates also to the conservation program which apparently is being pursued with such vigour by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources in the north country.
I believe the time has come when we must pay some attention to conservation in the southern regions of Canada as well and I refer particularly to choice gardens and fruit lands in the southern part of our nation which year by year are being eaten away by industrial expansion and by housing and other developments. There are many areas

in this country which cannot produce the fruit and vegetables which will some day be required by our increased population as envisaged and referred to so often by the Prime Minister and the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources and it behooves us to take steps to protect the land that is suitable for the purpose of growing fruit and vegetables. It is distressing to see areas like the Niagara peninsula which is a veritable garden being used purely for industrial purposes. Unless some action is taken all the desirable fruit and vegetable growing areas of Canada will be the site of industrial expansion when there are other sections of the country not suitable for growing things where the industries could be located. The great vision of Canada with a population of between 50 and 100 million in the future will never be realized unless some care and planning is undertaken to ensure that we will be able to take advantage of the resources of our country.

subtopic: AMENDMENT INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT AVAILABLE, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, before I make a few observations on this resolution I should like to join with others who have spoken before me in paying tribute not only to the officials of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation who are present with us today but also to their staffs across the country. I have had some dealings with the employees of C.M.H.C. and I have found them to be dedicated people who are doing a tremendous job for the good of this country. Last year it was my privilege to serve on a housing committee. We visited the headquarters of the corporation and were shown their activities. We were given every assistance in understanding their problems. I can assure this committee that the government is indeed fortunate in having people of the calibre it has handling the affairs of C.M.H.C.
I was very much interested in certain figures the minister gave us particularly as they applied to the arguments advanced by the hon. member for Nipissing. It appears that in 1955 C.M.H.C. mortgages represented 2.6 per cent of total mortgage monies loaned and in 1958 it increased to 42.3 per cent. The minister told us the total housing starts in 1958 were 164,642. According to my figures this represents an increase of 18 per cent over the previous record year of 1955. It is interesting to compare these figures with comparable figures for the United States. Housing starts there were down 13 per cent in 1958 from 1955.
As I understood his remarks the hon. member for Nipissing attempted to say it is all very well for the government to provide mortgage funds but the greater portion of
National Housing Act
these would have been available from private sources in any event but I believe these figures indicate this is not the case. It has only been the action of this government that has enabled the housing program to contribute to our economy in the way it has.
I recall attending the national home builders convention in Toronto in 1957 which was addressed by the Minister of Public Works. At that time he set a target of 140,000 housing starts for 1958. The projected number of starts for 1958 was 90,000. The builders who were assembled and who had come from one end of Canada to the other, out of deference to the minister, did not state their views as bluntly as perhaps they might have done but the general consensus was, "well, this is impossible." But, as the minister has informed us the actual figure for 1958 was over 164,000 housing starts.
The employment this program has provided in Canada cannot be too strongly emphasized. The construction, supply of materials, and furnishings represented by this program in terms of dollar value has the greatest labour content of any activity one could imagine and not only does it have the greatest labour content per dollar expended but it represents the greatest Canadian content. From every point of view, therefore, the house-building program has been an aid and impetus to the economy of the country not only in terms of providing on-site work in some thousands of municipalities across the country but also in terms of providing a backlog of orders for manufacturing centres in the industrial heart of Canada.
In view of this I can readily sympathize with the opposition in its attempt to find some weakness to attack with a view to offering constructive criticism. As far as I can ascertain hon. members of the opposition are trying to do something that is practically impossible. I suggest that they give whole-hearted support to this measure and have very little more to say so that it may be put through and we may get on to something else where the ground may be somewhat more fruitful for them.
I am indeed pleased that amendments are being introduced to permit an expansion of the activities of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation particularly in the mortgage field. They will now be able to buy and sell mortgages. The next step might be to enter the mortgage bond field. They could have a ready market across the country as is the case in the United Kingdom. The present amendments represent a long step forward and should relieve the corporation of some of the difficulties it has encountered in securing sufficient monies from various sources in the country.

National Housing Act
The same type of thinking, of course, was behind the amendment which raises the insurance value from 98 to 100 per cent. However, I am particularly interested in the limited dividend type of housing as handled by the corporation. Total monies spent to date in that field were $117 million of which $52 million have been expended since January 1, 1958, comprising some 7,000 rental units. This was an increase from 4,100 rental units in 1957. As far as I can determine there was little activity in this field prior to the last two years. In my opinion this is a field which should invite development and expansion. I believe the corporation will have extra revenue because of its increased activities. It may well be that the corporation could establish a promotional or developmental section of the organization which could advise service clubs, church groups and others how they could participate in the limited dividend type of housing.
There is a growing need for this type of accommodation. In addition to projects for old age pensioners there is a severe need for housing for low income groups which must be partially subsidized in order to have reasonable housing. This is the field in which there is much yet to be done. I give the corporation full credit for the rather fantastic increase in the number of units which have been completed in the last few years; but I do suggest that it is in this area that a great deal more might be done by pushing the people who can do it. I know that the corporation cannot initiate it. All I am saying is that the corporation can help other people to initiate it.
I was rather struck by the fact that the great proportion of money spent in this field has been spent in the central provinces, where perhaps greater activity has taken place and where they may be closer to a certain amount of persuasion from the head office of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
I was rather surprised to hear the hon. member for Timmins say that the corporation's standards did not meet local building standards. Certain complaints have come to me from builders to the effect that the corporation's standards are too high. This is the first time I have ever had any indication that the corporation's standards were lower than other standards in the country. Frankly, I can hardly credit it. I think there must be some misconception in this regard. The hon. member for Timmins might check up on this point.
I do not want to take up very much time, Mr. Chairman, but I do wish to say how much I appreciate the operations of the corporation, and I am grateful for the way in which the government has stood behind the

corporation and provided the money for this tremendously expanded and increased housing program. It has meant much to the country and it has meant more particularly to my province of British Columbia. I know mill after mill which is totally dependent upon the housing industry, and I am quite sure there are many factories in Ontario making all sorts of equipment used in houses which are also pretty well 100 per cent dependent on this industry. I say that the government has shown great foresight and has planned very well. It is pleasing to know that the money will be spent as advantageously as possible to provide the greatest amount of employment to the end that Canadians will have decent living standards.

subtopic: AMENDMENT INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT AVAILABLE, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we welcome this legislation as a continuation of a policy which has kept the house-building industry at a very high level, and which has undoubtedly created a great deal of additional employment in many parts of the country at a time when the economy was not as full as it had been previously.
I was glad to hear the minister say today that the policy had been a small home loan policy, because on previous occasions I have heard it referred to as a low-cost loan policy. I think he is correct today when he refers to it as a small home loan policy.
The minister has asked for suggestions and I know that any suggestions that are made will be considered by him. I think the limitation of 1,050 square feet, with which I do not quarrel because they have to draw an arbitrary line somewhere, is too low in some instances. As the minister knows-if he does not know his officials can tell him-the 1,050 square feet in a bungalow may cost $10.50 a square foot to build, whereas the next 100 square feet might cost only $5 per foot to build, and it is the next 100 square feet which is in fact the low-cost part of the house. Therefore, in some areas at least this arbitrary limitation is not working to the benefit of prospective house purchasers. For instance, in Toronto, at the price of lots at the present time, I do not think it is right to put a house as small as 1,050 square feet on a lot as expensive as the ones within the metropolitan area.
The minister indicated that one of the main objectives was maintaining high employment and I think that that objective has been met very well. However, I think caution is necessary, Mr. Speaker, in relation to the possible effects of trying to build too many houses too quickly. I know the minister did not intend it to be so, but this money was, in fact, to many people in our area at least manna from heaven for the speculators.

If we go back to 1956 we find that the price of raw land had dropped about 25 per cent in that area. The price held more or less steady in the following year, 1957, but last year, after the government made its announcement that large sums of money would be made available, the price of raw land in the metropolitan area and in the outskirts of Toronto increased at least 25 per cent in one year. It might also interest the minister to know that last summer the industry was beyond its physical capacity. We had a definite demonstration of that when for a considerable length of time it was impossible to get sufficient plastering crews to complete houses on schedule. The result was that the cost of plastering small houses increased about 20 per cent in a matter of two weeks and for the first time since 1950 crews came on the job or wanted to come on the job, consisting of one plasterer and seven helpers, with a consequent down-grading in quality. Schedules were thrown out and it was not until some months after that the situation again came into equilibrium, when there were sufficient skilled tradesmen available to do the job that had to be done.
In addition, in the city of Toronto last year the price of lots increased by 25 per cent in one year. This is a round figure, but I am sure it is pretty close to the average. Lots in Scarborough, which were selling for $3,800 to $4,000 at the beginning of last year, were selling at the end of the year for $5,000 or $5,200. I noticed in last week's paper a suggestion of a number of the present Scarborough council members that the price this year will be of the order of $5,500. What has happened is that the total cost of small houses in Toronto has gone up by about 10 per cent in the last 12 months. The caution which is needed is that if this continues, or if this is a trend, the objective which the government has in mind will not be accomplished.
I asked for some figures to be sent down in respect to the persons who purchased our houses last year and as an exercise I worked out what would happen if the price of houses and the amount of the mortgage were increased by 10 per cent. The effect would be to reduce the market by 36 per cent and that is really quite a substantial reduction. If that is the trend and if higher prices reduce the total market and the number of qualified purchasers, then ultimately it will result in fewer houses being purchased and less employment, which is the opposite effect to that which the government hopes to achieve.
Undoubtedly part of the problem in the Toronto area at least is not directly attributable to the actions of the government but involves something in which they are very much
National Housing Act
interested. I refer to the relationships between the government and the municipalities. If the government would like to reverse the present trend, and I know they would, I think they could be of considerable assistance by making loans available to the municipalities for the installation of trunk facilities such as trunk sewers and water mains, sewage disposal plants, water filtration plants and so on. I believe this was talked about as part of the government's platform last year and it is an area in which they could be of very great assistance to the house building industry.
If the government would make assistance available on a widespread basis the municipalities would be able to permit the servicing of a great many additional areas of land and the prices of lots would come down because they reflect the law of supply and demand very closely. I am sure that if additional lots were available and the price came down, as I am convinced it would, the market for housing would increase and the government would then be able to accomplish what it has in mind. I am sure they would find no difficulty in working out arrangements with the municipalities to effect such a program, and I hope the government will take that into consideration at a very early date.
Another question which was raised by the hon. member for Nipissing is where the government is going to get the money for its additional program. As the minister said, and I quote him, "Personally I cannot think of a better way for a government to spend its money." I know that the minister realizes that the government has no money of its own but must get it from somewhere, and if it gets it from the banks or other lending institutions which otherwise might invest it in insured housing loans then the total supply of housing is not increased. If, on the other hand, it gets the money from the banking system, through the mechanics of the Bank of Canada, then it is in competition with other government cash requirements. This is something about which the government will certainly have to be somewhat cautious.
With reference to the limited dividend section of the housing act, I think we are all pleased that greater use of this facility is taking place at the present time. I am one who has always thought that the section should be used much more widely than it was and I am very pleased that such now seems to be the case. I sometimes wonder how Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation in making its evaluations now gets around its own regulations but undoubtedly it has devised some workable system. I will only say that I would be happier if they would change the regulations so that the invested

National Housing Act
equity of the entrepreneur would be reduced to 5 per cent in order that valuations could be strict and would not have to take into account enhanced land values.
I think the government deserves full marks for its efforts in the housing field but I believe greater discussion should take place on the possibility of getting costs down. In my opinion this is most important. I do not like to seem old-fashioned in worrying about costs but I think the future of the industry and the need to make better housing available for all Canadians require that we give this aspect of the problem greater consideration and more thought. Finally, I think allowances have to be made for a "Green" administration. However, now that the government has been in office 18 months and there are no elections in the immediate offing we expect that this program will continue with greater finesse.

subtopic: AMENDMENT INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT AVAILABLE, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not want to delay the passing of the resolution but I should like to add my words to those of the hon. member for Vancouver South concerning the minister and the officials and staff of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. I thought that both the hon. member for Vancouver South and the minister were extremely modest in their remarks. To deal first with the hon. member for Vancouver South, I think that his efforts in providing the stimulus for a housing committee and his energetic activity in promoting interest among members of the house and spreading the word about limited dividend housing should be mentioned so that they will go on the record of the house.
As far as the minister is concerned, his estimate of the number of jobs created by 164,642 houses is at least 100,000 less than the most conservative estimate I have been able to obtain from government sources or from the industry. He referred to 200,000 on-site and 200,000 off-site jobs. The rock bottom figure I have been able to obtain, on the basis of calculation by people in that field, is 500,000. My imagination and ability to project were staggered when the minister mentioned the figure of $1,700 to $2,000 as the cost of services and equipment accompanying the erection of each housing unit. I did some very fast arithmetic and came up with the figure of $329 million. I boggle at the task of having to estimate how many jobs are created in the process of manufacturing the goods to meet this demand.
I was also most pleased, in fact, delighted to note the increase to 7,000 units under the limited dividend section of the act. I should like to think that the amount of housing

activity in my riding during the last year was due perhaps in part at least to the minister's good will toward me, but while he may feel that way I am afraid the real explanation is that virtually the only open land east of Yonge street available for housing in the metropolitan Toronto area is in my riding, and entrepreneurs such as the hon. member for Trinity are very active in that regard.
I should like to refer briefly to the land assembly aspect of housing and to encourage the government to increase its activities in co-operation with the province in this area with a view perhaps to bringing about a reduction in the cost of land, serviced or otherwise, as mentioned by the hon. member for Trinity. I should like to make a specific recommendation to the minister on the matter of land assembly. When in co-operation with the province certain land is assembled and designated for low cost or low rental housing I would recommend that such land be marked by signs clearly visible from the perimeter of the area so that it will be impossible for developers, promoters and sellers of houses in the immediate area surrounding such land to avoid telling purchasers of homes for what purpose the adjacent land is designated.
There have been cases in my riding where, from talking to the occupants of certain homes adjacent to limited dividend or land assembly schemes, it would seem that statements by real estate salesmen have indicated that the land was going to be a park or a green belt or something which would add tremendously to the value of their homes. I repeat that I should like to see action taken to have signs erected, clearly visible from the adjacent areas, indicating the purpose for which it is intended to use the land. Any purchaser of a house will not object to certain situations developing in the neighbourhood so long as he is aware that they will develop in connection with the land adjacent to his home when he purchases his home.
Another problem which I am afraid is beyond the scope of this house or this government relates to the social conscience of those who live in areas adjacent to low cost or low rental land assembly areas. I think it is fair to say that when the provincial and federal governments assemble land on the perimeter of our urban areas the development of that land must await the movement of services out beyond the developed land in the immediate area. I would urge the individuals already occupying or who are going to occupy those areas as a result of government action to endorse and approve the establishment of further low cost units

or senior citizens' units. Unhappily, in this city and the city of Toronto and in other metropolitan areas the actions of ratepayers and others in this regard have been something less than the best demonstration of social conscience.
I should like to refer very briefly before I resume my seat to the remarks of the hon. member for Timmins. He deplored the fact that individuals in the lower income group were not being effectively assisted by this legislation. I did some more fast arithmetic on the basis of the figures the minister gave us and found that over 80 per cent of the loans made went to the group with $5,999 and under annual income and that 56.1 per cent went to the group with $4,999 and under annual income. The hon. member for Trinity if I heard him correctly, made perhaps the most preposterous criticism to come from the other side of this house in this session. If I understood his comments, he was suggesting it was the fault of this government's program because too many jobs had been created in the housing industry. If that is the type of complaint we can expect from an hon. member with long experience in the housing field I think it is fair to say that this government has done a truly remarkable job.

subtopic: AMENDMENT INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT AVAILABLE, ETC.
speechtext:
I wish, first of all, to join with those who preceded me in extending congratulations to the Minister of Public Works for promoting this house-building program. I wish to give the government credit for the introduction of this resolution, the effect of which would be to enable Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to invest an additional $250 million to provide an expanded housing program which is sorely needed in Canada today. This agency, which was first established by the former Liberal government, has a creditable record in the construction of rental housing.
I think we can all agree, in fact every speaker who preceded me has agreed, upon the need for housing today. Housing remains the basic need of communities, especially a community such as Fort William. In the growing and vigorous towns and cities it is almost impossible to find a house for rent, especially if the applicant has a large family. I am a firm believer in a policy of making money available at the lower rate of interest for the construction of homes.
During the throne speech debate in the last session of parliament I had this to say with regard to housing and I believe it is still applicable. I am quoting from page 351 of Hansard for May 22, 1958:
With respect to housing, the speech contained the promise of a vigorous program of house-building.
National Housing Act
However, the legislation adopted in the house last week did not go far enough. My own view is that the government should subsidize interest rates on mortgage loans for houses costing less than $12,000. Anybody who is able to afford a new house costing over $12,000 should be able to meet the going market interest rate. Houses, including site costs, under $12,000 are today in the low cost category and a subsidy of say two per cent would bring the effective rate of interest to about four per cent.
One of the crying needs of the moment is houses for rent. In our municipality we have taken advantage of the former government's housing scheme introduced in 1950 or 1951, and I was pleased to see that the present government is carrying on with the same formula of 75 per cent federal investment and 25 per cent split between the province and the municipality. The only trouble is that the scheme, while good, should provide for an increase in the federal government's share of the cost of acquiring and clearing substandard areas for low rental housing projects.
I am still in favour of that proposal that a lower interest rate should be made available for housing projects for low income groups.
There is another thing I want to bring to the attention of this house, and which I think is very important. I would urge that an investigation be made of the financial capabilities of the people now occupying homes erected under the National Housing Act, to make sure that people who are renting these subsidized homes are not people who can afford to provide their own accommodation. I have reason to believe that there are many who are now in homes subsidized by the three levels of government whose income does not qualify them for consideration for this type of housing, while others with low income and probably with large families cannot find accommodation of any kind. I know of families living in garages, summer cottages, attics and basements, while some with incomes between $4,000 and $6,000 a year are occupying houses which were built to accommodate those who cannot afford to buy or to rent from private enterprise.
The latter constitutes the largest group for which our government should direct Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to build houses, because in spite of the increased housing construction during the past year- for which I wish to compliment the government-a backlog of unfilled housing need still remains. All you have to do is to add up all the marriages taking place in communities. In our community of Fort William there is an average of approximately 600 marriages a year. We never had more than 400 houses built in the best of construction years. There you have the situation. We are not providing sufficient accommodation, irrespective of whatever may be said to the contrary by some people who may find themselves in communities where the housing

National Housing Act
situation may be better. I am speaking for my own community and communities with which I-am familiar.
I should also like to point out that loans for housing purposes should be made available to small communities such as those in my own riding like Kakabeka Falls, Murillo, Hymers, Nolalu and others, with a population of a few hundred and which, to my knowledge, have been unable to get any loan from any quarter. In other words, they have been ignored. There is no question that thousands of our people, in both urban and rural districts, are living today in substandard houses. Many are living in shacks which are hardly fit for human habitation.
I am certainly in favour of funds being made available as called for in this resolution. I urge that they be used for the purpose of stimulating the construction of homes which the low income bracket group can afford to buy or to rent. I agree with the Minister of Public Works when he says that there is no better way in which to spend government money than on housing.

Mr. Chairman, I am sure that my remarks will be brief, as no hon. member would like to hold up the passing of this resolution. For that reason alone I think encouragement of the housing industry is extremely important to us.
The minister has made a complete resume of the housing industry and the job that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has done. I should just like to ask a couple of questions in reference to parts of the resolution. Perhaps the minister will answer them when he closes the discussion. There was some question of legislation permitting the sale of mortgages that are held by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. I should be greatly interested in learning whether there is any likelihood of a discount proposition being considered. I think this is a pertinent question and one of principle. speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENT INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT AVAILABLE, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the debate this afternoon has been extremely helpful. I must say that everyone who has spoken has put forward ideas which will be given careful consideration. In my opinion, this has been one of the best debates we have had in
the house for a long time. I do not intend to try to answer all the points which have been raised during the course of the afternoon. However, there are one or two things which I think should be dealt with.
The hon. member for Nipissing in the course of his thought-provoking speech, asked what percentage of this additional money would go into small homes. Under the policy all of the money would go into small homes or low rental projects under the limited dividend provision except where direct loans are made by the corporation to a person wishing to build a home in a smaller centre. As the hon. member knows, these loans have been handled directly by the corporation for some time. There might be some of these homes which would be over the area of 1,050 square feet.
Mention was also made of the need to keep the cost of housing down. This suggestion came from the hon. member for Trinity. We are always doing whatever is possible in that direction. Each year the Canadian construction association calls a conference to consider the small home problem. At this conference are representatives of the banks and lending institutions, the architects, engineers, municipalities and Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. A great deal of thought has been put on ways of keeping down the costs. In view of the fact that there has been a trend of steadily rising prices in every field, I think the cost of houses has been kept down as much as was reasonably possible. In some metropolitan areas, particularly in Toronto, the costs are much higher than they are anywhere else in Canada. It is particularly difficult to meet this situation. At the moment I do not know quite how it is going to be done.
Hon. members might be interested to learn that of the $750 million which has been provided by legislation to date approximately $45 million has been repaid. This particular $750 million is not a revolving fund. The corporation must get authority to commit these funds. However, when it gets cash back it must pay that cash to the Department of Finance and there is no credit against the total authorized expenditure. Hence in effect there is only about $705 million actually outstanding. As time goes on, of course, more and more money will be coming back. This is one of the good features of the plan. We shall have to devise some way for Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and the Minister of Public Works to get some credit for the money that comes back.
The other points which have been made during the course of the debate will be given careful consideration by the officials of the corporation and also by myself.

In regard to the answer to the question asked by the hon. member for Muskoka-Parry Sound, if Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation does decide to dispose of mortgages it will be done at the going market price. This would depend, for example, on the interest rate of the particular mortgage and on the demand for mortgages at the time. I am afraid it is impossible to give him any idea as to what extent this power will be exercised. The corporation has had power right along to sell mortgages to approved lenders only. Under the proposed legislation it will be able to sell to other companies which are not approved lenders provided the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation continues to administer the loans. I cannot give the hon. member a more definite answer than that.

Mr. Chairman, it was not my intention to take the floor this afternoon, but since all matters pertaining to the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation are of particular interest to the constituency I represent, I should like to take this opportunity to express my views.
Mr. Chairman, if we consider the purpose of the previous government in setting up the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, we realize that it was to provide our citizens with houses and not jobs. The Conservative party has made it a social security measure. The corporation now has a double purpose: that of providing houses as well as jobs.
When the previous administration froze housing credits, the result was an economic disorder from which we are still suffering today. Since the building and housing industry has slowed down, tradesmen have become the first victims. Then there has been a certain recession which has had the effect, as you no doubt know, of creating an alarming unemployment problem.
The consequences of the Conservative party's easing credit facilities in favour of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, have instilled a new activity in industry and trades, and this has contributed, to some extent, to create jobs for Canadian workers.
We would face a sad plight if the Conservative party had not pledged itself to protect the interest of its voters by increasing credit facilities which the previous administration had neutralized through a short-sighted policy.
Mr. Chairman, if there are some disadvantages to the present National Housing Act, it
National Housing Act
certainly provides certain benefits, especially for the working class. I represent a constituency where the majority are working people. Those workers depend on their trade for their living and if construction activity had not been promoted through increased housing credits, our working population would find itself in a very deplorable situation. But if generally speaking the act helps the working class, it has not rectified certain irregularities concerning the workers.
